newsitem.title: INDIA: India says 150,000 child workers rehabilitated.
newsitem.headline: India says 150,000 child workers rehabilitated.

text.p: India has taken 150,000 child labourers out of hazardous industries under a plan to eliminate child labour from such jobs by 2002, Labour Minister M. Arunachalam was quoted on Friday as saying.

"So far we have taken out 150,000 children from hazardous industries. By the year 2002, child labour will be eliminated altogether from such industrial units," the minister told the Financial Express newspaper in an interview.

Under pressure from Western trading nations, which have considered trade sanctions linked to the use of child labour, in 1994 India launched a state-funded programme to take out children from harmful industries and send them to school.

India and some other developing countries oppose trade curbs linked to child labour and say Western nations are using the issue to gain unfair trade advantages. But New Delhi has simultaneously launched steps to blunt their criticism.
Arunachalam said the government spent 350 million rupees ($10 million) in 1995/96 (April-March), and had earmarked 560 million rupees for 1996/97 to rehabilitate child labourers.
"They are being put in a special school and a stipend is being given to their parents to compensate for their earnings," he was quoted as saying.
Child labour is legally banned in India except in situations where children help their families in agricultural work or in traditional cottage industries.
But child labour is widespread, and child workers are a common sight in several industries.
India's labour ministry puts the number of child labourers at 18 million out of an estimated population of 930 million. Activist groups say the figure is around 55 million.
"We have to tackle the root cause (of child labour) first. The number one provocation is illiteracy, followed by parental poverty, unemployment and underemployment," Arunachalam said.
"These problems have to be tackled first and the government is giving a lot of attention to these issues."
The goverment says its first priority is to eliminate child labour from harmful industries like firework making, stone quarrying, glass and chemical industries.

Western consumer groups have targeted the handwoven carpet industry for possible trade sanctions. Activists say that India, Pakistan, and Nepal together account for estimated 1.2 million children working in carpet factories.
